report:
Codex PASS lacked valid task or source evidence for every premise. PASS applies to the retained partial results and the mathematical gap analysis in n1–n4. It does not certify the original P13.2 image or existence characterization. I checked the supplied argument, notes, source excerpts, and relevant context in the four exact public PDF versions. Operational observations and artifact preservation were excluded.

Torification is valid. After quotienting by the prime kernel of a semivaluation, the Gauss coefficient-minimum valuation on the Laurent polynomial ring is multiplicative: nonzero initial Laurent polynomials multiply nontrivially over the graded residue domain. Pullback through the action homomorphism gives the stated formula. Homogeneous evaluations remain unchanged, the character-matrix argument identifies the invariant locus, and finite minima give continuity. Thus τ preserves X0, fixes K, and is idempotent. The compactness proof concerns the carrier: v(𝔪)=0 excludes negative evaluations using gʳh∈𝔪; the resulting semivaluation space and finite-generator link condition are closed in a compact product. Factorization through τ survives uniform and decreasing limits. No potential-space compactness follows.

The model-support argument survives the stated facet correction. Equivariance supplies a common Hessian kernel, so the top homogeneous mixed wedge vanishes; “Hessian zero” must mean singular. The full-hyperplane identity is genuinely false near (0,1) for max{x,y}. In its actual application, the normalized reference linear forms have the same nonzero Reeb-direction derivative. Consequently the relevant boundary consists of oriented active facets, and coincident facet forms have identical gradients. Remove radial smoothing first while the other factors remain smooth. Convex finite-difference bounds then give the required gradient traces; facet intersections have zero ordinary facet measure at this stage. Subsequently removing the remaining smoothing gives mixed PL curvature supported at finitely many vertices of the transverse polyhedral subdivision. This establishes local discreteness without using the defective full-hyperplane formula. Compactness makes support finite. The action on this support factors through a finite abelian quotient of divisible T(k), hence is trivial. Continuous and decreasing finite-energy approximation preserve probability mass and support on closed K. These applications use the normal-cone hypotheses, not smoothness or klt assumptions. [Wu21](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.13395v2), [Wu24](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.13684v1).

The density proof is correct on K. Same-ray continuous-potential addition puts both terms of the displayed maximum identity at ab/(a+b)ξ; scaling and interchange establish the real vector-space operations. The separating test retains the reference generators and handles infinite evaluations. Compactness, constants, and the lattice operations give uniform density. This can also be verified by the usual finite-cover proof of lattice Stone–Weierstrass. A source-proof qualification matters here: literal FS addition requires commensurable coefficients; rational ξ alone does not make arbitrary real a/b commensurable. The continuous addition rule actually used remains valid by rational coefficient-ratio approximation after clearing degrees, followed by the individual Reeb approximation. No FS closure under irrational addition is required. The two A² semivaluations in the full-link counterexample agree on every homogeneous test but differ on x−y. The energy maximum bound gives both Dirac measures dual energy zero, while the carrier excludes δw as an output. Thus the counterexample and the corrected domains of the density assertions are valid.

The normalization is consistent throughout the retained proof: n−1 potential factors, one radial factor, division by Vξ, and n energy summands with denominator nVξ. Translation gives E(φ+c)=E(φ)+c and the dual expression changes by (1−m)c, forcing mass one. Scaling ξ along its own ray gives the stated volume, current, and energy identities. For c>0, the polynomial-cone degree filtration has potential ρ+c, energy c, truncated mean cn/(n+1), and equal-degree mean c. These are the actual Wu21 definitions, so the printed E=S identification conflicts within that version. Likewise its printed slice formula, with the explicitly stated slice mass Vξ, returns c/(n+1). These discrepancies cannot be dismissed as a version change or an unstated slice-measure convention.

The supporting signs are correct. For continuous potentials, successive mixed integrals differ by nonnegative Hodge norms, so their average lies between the endpoint integrals. The second variation includes dd u and the coefficient n−1. For E1, decreasing continuity applies to each integral separately; integrability makes their differences legitimate. Consequently E∨(MA(φ))=E(φ)−∫φ MA(φ), and every genuine output satisfies the finite homogeneous FS test. The reversed supporting inequality in Wu24 is a real printed defect. Its I–J displays also require consistent reversal of the mixed-term index: with j counting φ factors, the Jψ(φ) coefficient is (n−1−j)/n. This leaves the retained bounds I/n≤J≤(n−1)I/n unchanged. The three-point quasi-triangle inequality used here is the correct one printed in Proposition 6.8(4), rather than the repeated-index display in Theorem 4.5.

The Radon net lemma has the needed exact scope: K is compact Hausdorff, μ is a finite positive Radon measure, the functions are finite continuous functions decreasing pointwise, and the limit is upper semicontinuous with values in R∪{−∞}. An initial function supplies an eventual upper bound. Regularity gives the infimum over continuous majorants. Directedness and compactness turn the increasing open cover {fi<g+ε} into one covering index. For a general finite measure, the error is ε μ(K); the submission’s ε shorthand is correct in its probability application. This proves the lemma including integral −∞, without countable monotone convergence. Energy continuity then proves equality of the FS and E1 dual suprema. Finite dual energy forces every E1 potential to be integrable. None of this passes an unbounded test through an arbitrary weak limit.

The repaired mixed estimate is correct. Concavity gives −B≤E(φ̄), and nonpositivity of every energy summand gives E(φ̄)≤n⁻¹∫φ̄ MA(φ̄). The comparison φ̄≤φ0/n and the mixed expansion yield E(φ̄)≤(n−1)! n⁻(n+1)∫φ0 MA(φ1,…,φn−1). Thus the constant is exactly n^(n+1)/(n−1)!. This bound also supplies the finite uniform lower bounds needed in the source’s finite-energy induction: keep the tested approximant continuous during weak convergence, then use the Radon lemma. The lower bound for simultaneous decreasing pairings follows from integration by parts and the lower-induction error terms. The corrected density and this estimate therefore address the source defects relevant to the finite-energy applications; arbitrary weak target integration is not being assumed.

The maximizing-sequence estimates follow exactly as stated. The midpoint belongs to CPSH(ξ), even when it need not be FS. The two J bounds and the quasi-triangle inequality give midpoint energy gain at least I(φ,ψ)/(2nQn). Cancelling target integrals bounds this gain by half the sum of the deficits. Hence I(φj,φk)≤nQn(Δj+Δk). Taking ψ=ρ and using the upper J bound gives Jρ(φj)≤(n−1)Qn(Δj+E∨(μ)). The source quasi-triangle estimate can be reconstructed from Hodge seminorms, Cauchy–Schwarz, and convexity of J with its reference fixed; joint convexity of I is unnecessary. Output bi-Lipschitzness gives an I∨-Cauchy output sequence. It provides neither a genuine limit potential nor identification with μ. Uniqueness and image comparison are retained directly as task-granted inputs; global separation of arbitrary measures is not inferred.

Both toric computations check independently. The soft maximum has Hessian determinant integral 1/r!, while its superform wedge contributes r!, giving transverse mass one. The radial soft positive part also has mass one. A coordinate matrix C contributes |det C|. In A², the curvature intersection is (0,s), its coefficient is one, V=1, and the energy terms are s and 0, giving E(φs)=s/2 and the claimed sign counterexample. In A³, the Reeb-simplex count gives V=1/√6. The squared homogeneous curvature lies on the stated line, the radial cut meets it only at w=(0,√2,√3), and the displayed coordinate matrix has determinant magnitude 1/√6. Thus the unnormalized current is (1/√6)δw and the normalized measure is δw. At coordinate boundaries, a term disappears and the remaining homogeneous curvature has rank at most one, so its square contributes no boundary mass. The atom is monomial on the stratum where x1 is a unit, has value group √2 Z+√3 Z of rational rank two, and cannot be a real rescaling of a divisorial valuation.

The necessary dimension clarification is harmless: Hessian and Hodge formulas containing n−2 apply for n≥2. A one-dimensional normal good effective torus cone is A¹. Its invariant link is a singleton, genuine potentials restrict to constants, E(c)=c, the operator has no potential factors, and I=J=0. The mixed bound and maximizing-sequence bounds then hold directly. No positive-dimensional synthetic theorem is applied at this endpoint.

The mathematical findings in n4 are accurate for this argument and its four sources. Projective compactness uses the envelope property; the projective completeness/surjectivity equivalence also uses target integration continuity and variational identification. Uniform differentiation uses projective relative volumes and added polarizations. Proposition 9.19 obtains target integration continuity through uniform approximation by model outputs, whose target identification uses differentiation. Its final max identity has the harmless algebraic correction |a−b|=2(max{a,b}−b)−(a−b). These projective results are not automatically cone results. Smoothness is required by the cited projective existence theorem; normal rational quotients need not be smooth. The model quotient comparisons do not establish general invariant finite-energy realization. [BJ22](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1801.08229v4).

The synthetic conclusions require the full ordered-form formalism and the actual orthogonality limit. Their density and completeness concern measures, and do not supply Wu finite-energy potentials. Finite maxima, individual Reeb approximation, one-sided admissible variations, and output comparison do not establish the missing antecedents or the requested realization. The constrained-maximizer example correctly demonstrates why a one-sided derivative inequality does not identify the target. The gap analysis makes no claim that newer literature is absent. All mathematical assertions of n1–n4 are therefore supported within the stated partial scope. [BJ23](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.01697v1).

passages.statement: For a positive-dimensional normal polarized affine cone (X,T;ξ) over an algebraically closed trivially valued characteristic-zero field, Vξ=limm→∞ n!m⁻ⁿ∑⟨ξ,α⟩≤m dim Rα exists and is positive and finite. Homogeneous FS functions are psh-approachable; their positive mixed currents are continuous under local uniform approximation. The current ddφ1∧⋯∧ddφn−1∧ddρ⁺ has finite atomic support on invariant points of {ρ=0}, and division by Vξ gives a probability measure. In tropical moment charts these currents are represented by the corresponding superform wedges with the chart calibration. Wu21, Definition 2.4, Proposition 5.4 and Corollary 5.7; Wu24, Theorem 2.12.

passages.statement: For a normal polarized affine cone of dimension n≥2 over an algebraically closed trivially valued characteristic-zero field, integration by parts holds for invariant differences of continuous same-ray psh potentials against mixed continuous psh currents and ddρ⁺. The associated invariant-difference bilinear forms are seminegative and satisfy Cauchy–Schwarz. For continuous ξ-psh potentials, E(φ)=(nVξ)⁻¹∑j=0n−1∫(φ−ρ)(ddφ)j(ddρ)n−1−j ddρ⁺ satisfies the energy cocycle identity, monotonicity, concavity, translation by constants, and the first variation ∫u MA(φ) along admissible segments. The successive mixed terms in the energy difference are non-increasing. Wu24, Propositions 3.8–3.9 and 4.2, restricted to invariant differences.

passages.statement: For a normal polarized affine cone over an algebraically closed trivially valued characteristic-zero field, every genuine ξ-psh function is a decreasing pointwise limit of homogeneous FS functions. Decreasing limits of ξ-psh functions are ξ-psh unless identically −∞. Genuine psh functions are finite at quasimonomial points of the link, and are determined by their quasimonomial evaluations. The energy defined as the infimum of energies of continuous psh majorants is monotone, translation-invariant in the stated additive sense, concave, upper semicontinuous in the quasimonomial-evaluation topology, and continuous along decreasing nets with psh limit. passages.statement: For an irreducible projective variety over a trivially valued field and a numerical class θ, the projective envelope property is equivalent to compactness of normalized PSH(θ) and to convergence of bounded-above increasing psh nets. For an ample class it is also equivalent to continuity of envelopes of continuous obstacles. If the projective variety is smooth and connected and either the field has characteristic zero or its dimension is at most two, nef classes have the envelope property. Under the corresponding smoothness and characteristic/dimension hypotheses, every finite-energy probability measure admits a projective finite-energy Monge–Ampère solution, unique modulo constants. BJ22, Theorems 5.11, 5.20 and 12.9, and Lemma 5.17.

For ω≥0 with [ω] in the interior of the image of Z+ in Z/ddD and Vω>0, put Dω={φ∈D:ω+ddφ≥0}, MAω(φ)=Vω⁻¹(ω+ddφ)d, and use the corresponding normalized mixed-sum energy and its dual measure energy. If Dω admits maxima, orthogonality—limφ∈Dω,<f∫(f−φ)MAω(φ)=0 for every f∈D—is equivalent to the uniform two-sided extended-energy differentiation estimate of Proposition 2.19. premises: For a positive-dimensional normal polarized affine cone (X,T;ξ) over an algebraically closed trivially valued characteristic-zero field, Vξ=limm→∞ n!m⁻ⁿ∑⟨ξ,α⟩≤m dim Rα exists and is positive and finite. Homogeneous FS functions are psh-approachable; their positive mixed currents are continuous under local uniform approximation. The current ddφ1∧⋯∧ddφn−1∧ddρ⁺ has finite atomic support on invariant points of {ρ=0}, and division by Vξ gives a probability measure. In tropical moment charts these currents are represented by the corresponding superform wedges with the chart calibration. Wu21, Definition 2.4, Proposition 5.4 and Corollary 5.7; Wu24, Theorem 2.12.

On every normal polarized affine cone over an algebraically closed trivially valued characteristic-zero field, CPSH(ξ) is the local uniform closure of H(ξ). It is stable under constants and maxima; aφ∈CPSH(ξ/a) for a>0; and φ∈CPSH(aξ), ψ∈CPSH(bξ) imply φ+ψ∈CPSH(abξ/(a+b)) for a,b>0. It is convex. For φ∈CPSH(ξ) and any sequence of Reeb fields ξi→ξ, there are φi∈H(ξi) converging locally uniformly to φ. Wu24, Lemma 3.2 and Proposition 3.3.

For a normal polarized affine cone of dimension n≥2 over an algebraically closed trivially valued characteristic-zero field, integration by parts holds for invariant differences of continuous same-ray psh potentials against mixed continuous psh currents and ddρ⁺. The associated invariant-difference bilinear forms are seminegative and satisfy Cauchy–Schwarz. For continuous ξ-psh potentials, E(φ)=(nVξ)⁻¹∑j=0n−1∫(φ−ρ)(ddφ)j(ddρ)n−1−j ddρ⁺ satisfies the energy cocycle identity, monotonicity, concavity, translation by constants, and the first variation ∫u MA(φ) along admissible segments. The successive mixed terms in the energy difference are non-increasing. Wu24, Propositions 3.8–3.9 and 4.2, restricted to invariant differences.

For a normal polarized affine cone over an algebraically closed trivially valued characteristic-zero field, every genuine ξ-psh function is a decreasing pointwise limit of homogeneous FS functions. Decreasing limits of ξ-psh functions are ξ-psh unless identically −∞. Genuine psh functions are finite at quasimonomial points of the link, and are determined by their quasimonomial evaluations. The energy defined as the infimum of energies of continuous psh majorants is monotone, translation-invariant in the stated additive sense, concave, upper semicontinuous in the quasimonomial-evaluation topology, and continuous along decreasing nets with psh limit. Wu24, Proposition 5.2, Corollary 5.3, Theorem 5.8 and Proposition 5.10.

For a normal polarized affine cone of dimension n≥2 over an algebraically closed trivially valued characteristic-zero field, the model mixed operator extends to (n−1)-tuples in E1(ξ) as Radon probability measures on X0. Every E1 potential is integrable against every such mixed measure, and the pairing (ψ,φ1,…,φn−1)↦∫ψ MA(φ1,…,φn−1) is continuous when its arguments decrease to E1 limits. The mixed energy representation also extends to E1. Wu24, Theorem 6.3 and Corollary 6.6.

For a normal polarized affine cone of dimension n≥2 over an algebraically closed trivially valued characteristic-zero field, continuous and finite-energy potentials at fixed ξ satisfy I(φ,ψ)/n≤Jψ(φ)≤(n−1)I(φ,ψ)/n and I(φ,ψ)≤Qn(I(φ,θ)+I(θ,ψ)) for a dimensional constant Qn. Here I(φ,ψ)=∫(φ−ψ)(MA(ψ)−MA(φ)) and Jψ(φ)=E(ψ)−E(φ)+∫(φ−ψ)MA(ψ). Wu24, Proposition 6.8.

For a normal polarized affine cone over an algebraically closed trivially valued characteristic-zero field with primitive integral Reeb field ξ, the rational quotient is a normal projective polarized pair (V,BV;L). After passing to sufficiently divisible degrees, the homogeneous model functions considered in Wu21, Lemma 5.12, correspond to invariant FS metrics on L. Under the normalized embedding of Vᵃⁿ into the Reeb-invariant link, their mixed projective measures push forward to the cone mixed measures, their normalized energies agree, and vol(L)=Vξ. Wu21, Lemmas 3.16 and 5.11–5.12, Proposition 5.13 and Corollary 5.14.

Wu21 v2 defines Rm=⊕⟨ξ,α⟩≤m Rα and the truncated filtration invariant S as the limiting mean of jumping numbers divided by m dim Rm. In the integral rational case it defines the equal-degree invariant S̃ using H0(V,tL) and states S=nS̃/(n+1). In this same version, Theorem 5.15(1) prints Eᴺᴬ(φ)=S(F), and Theorem 6.3 prints Eᴺᴬ(χ)=((n+1)Vξ)⁻¹∫Pξ χ̃ dλ with λ(Pξ)=Vξ.

For an irreducible projective variety over a trivially valued field and a numerical class θ, the projective envelope property is equivalent to compactness of normalized PSH(θ) and to convergence of bounded-above increasing psh nets. For an ample class it is also equivalent to continuity of envelopes of continuous obstacles. If the projective variety is smooth and connected and either the field has characteristic zero or its dimension is at most two, nef classes have the envelope property. Under the corresponding smoothness and characteristic/dimension hypotheses, every finite-energy probability measure admits a projective finite-energy Monge–Ampère solution, unique modulo constants. BJ22, Theorems 5.11, 5.20 and 12.9, and Lemma 5.17.

For the projective pluripotential theory over a trivially valued field with an ample class ω, every f∈PL(X)R satisfies E↓(φ+εf)=E(φ)+ε∫f MA(φ)+O(ε²), uniformly in φ∈E1(ω). The extended energy equals envelope energy for continuous psh φ, and for all finite-energy φ when the envelope property holds. Maximizing nets for a finite-energy measure have model outputs converging weakly to that measure; computing the dual supremum is equivalent to solving its equation. A convergent psh net with eventually bounded J converges in L1 of every finite-energy measure. For an irreducible projective variety and an ample class, the envelope property, surjectivity, and strong completeness of E1(ω)/R are equivalent. BJ22, Theorem 8.5, Corollary 8.6, Theorem 9.11, Corollary 9.12, Proposition 9.19 and Theorem 12.8.
